sections.html:
Jenks is a Tulsa County suburb of Tulsa, set between the Arkansas River and U.S. Route 75. Population was 25,949 in the 2020 census and is estimated at 28,175 for July 2025, up from 16,924 in 2010. Growth that fast keeps buyers active, but the city runs its own permit office and ordinances, so local rules apply even when a buyer is shopping the whole metro.

Most of what a seller needs to sort out here comes down to four things: flood status, storm shelter paperwork, the county tax calendar and the state disclosure form. The sections below take them in that order.

Two numbers worth saving: the city permit office at 211 N Elm Street (inspections 918-299-5883) and the Tulsa County Assessor at 918-596-5100.

Floods from the Arkansas River and Polecat Creek hit Jenks again and again from 1904 through the 1950s. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers built a levee around the town in 1948, and a severe flood threat came back in 1986 when Keystone Dam releases reached up to 300,000 cubic feet per second.

That history is why buyers and lenders near the river or a creek ask about floodplain status early. The city requires a floodplain development permit for work in mapped floodplain areas, and its residential building permit form asks whether the property sits in a floodplain. If you have an elevation certificate or flood insurance paperwork, pull it before you list. It answers the question before anyone asks it.

Jenks regulates storm shelters through its permit office. You need a permit for an outdoor storm shelter, an in-ground safe room or an above-ground safe room built on site. Prefabricated above-ground safe rooms are exempt. Shelters must meet FEMA P-320 or ICC-500 standards and sit in the rear yard, outside setbacks and easements.

If you installed a shelter, find the permit and the manufacturer paperwork before you list. A permitted shelter that meets the standard is a feature a buyer can verify. An unpermitted one can raise questions at inspection. Applications are picked up at City Hall, second floor, 211 N Elm Street, or printed from the city's Protective Inspections page. Processing takes at least three working days.

sections.h2: Tulsa County property taxes when you sell
sections.html:
The Tulsa County Assessor values property as of January 1 each year and mails a notice whenever the fair cash value goes up. After a notice, you have 30 calendar days to protest in writing. Without an increase, you can still protest by the first Monday in April. Homestead applications must reach the assessor by March 15 or within 30 days of a valuation notice.

The Treasurer expects at least half of the tax before January 1 and the second half before April 1. If the first half is not paid before January 1, the whole amount becomes due and is treated as delinquent.

Tax stepRule
Valuation dateJanuary 1
Protest window30 days from notice, or by the first Monday in April
First-half paymentBefore January 1
Second-half paymentBefore April 1
Further appealBoard of Equalization, then District Court

Tell your buyer early about one change. When a home is purchased, the statutory cap on its taxable value comes off and the property is revalued every year, so the buyer's tax bill can differ from yours. Hand over your tax statement, and point the buyer to the assessor for the new figure.

If you sell part way through the year, the title company normally checks the treasurer's balance and splits or pays off what is owed from your proceeds. Selling between January and April, when the second half may still be open, is the case that needs the most attention. Ask for the payoff figure early so no surprise shows up at the table.

If you are behind on taxes, the same rule applies: a delinquent balance has to be cleared before the deed can move cleanly. Call the County Treasurer for the exact amount rather than guessing from an old statement.

Start with paperwork, then condition. Gather the tax statement, any floodplain or shelter permits, and the Oklahoma disclosure form. State law requires a seller to deliver a disclaimer or disclosure statement before the buyer's offer is accepted, and a buyer may sue if it is missing. The statute is 60 O.S. section 833 and the sections near it.

Then decide how fast you need to move. A listing can bring a financed buyer, but it comes with showings, inspections and a lender's timeline. A direct cash sale shortens the path and takes the house in the condition it is in, so repairs, cleanouts and appraisal delays drop out of the picture.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works from first call to closing
sections.html:
You call or send the address and we ask a few plain questions about the house: its condition, whether it is occupied, and whether any liens, back taxes or a mortgage payoff are involved. From that we make an offer. You compare it with what a listing would net after repairs, agent fees and carrying costs, and you take as long as you like to decide.

If you accept, a title company opens the file, runs the ownership and lien search and prepares the closing papers. You pick the closing date within reason, which helps if you are moving out of the Tulsa area or settling an estate. At closing you sign, the title company pays off any mortgage or tax balance from the proceeds, and you receive the rest. The house goes as it stands, with no showings, no buyer inspection requests and no lender approval to wait on.

Bring a photo ID, the mortgage lender's name if there is one, the latest tax statement and any permits for shelters or additions. Keys, garage openers and a short list of what stays or goes are all that is left to hand over.

sections.h2: What to tell us about your Jenks property
sections.html:
If the property sits in a mapped flood area, has an unpermitted addition or carries unpaid tax, say so up front so the offer reflects the real situation. It is also useful to know whether tenants live there, whether the house is vacant and whether anyone besides you has to sign.

Our editorial team writes these guides to explain choices. Any offer for a Jenks house is yours to accept or decline, and you can walk away at any point before you sign.

faqs.a: No. Jenks is its own city in Tulsa County and a suburb of Tulsa. Many Jenks school buildings are physically inside Tulsa, so the school district and the mailing city can differ.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a storm shelter in Jenks?
faqs.a: Yes for outdoor shelters, in-ground safe rooms and safe rooms built on site above ground. Prefabricated above-ground safe rooms do not need one. The shelter must meet FEMA P-320 or ICC-500, and processing takes at least three working days.

The city has a floodplain development permit process, and local history includes repeated floods before the 1948 levee and a flood threat in 1986. Check your parcel's floodplain status with the city at 918-299-5883.

faqs.q: What happens to my property tax cap when I sell a Jenks home?
faqs.a: The cap on taxable value comes off when a home is purchased. The buyer's first bill can be higher than yours, so share your tax statement and tell the buyer to confirm with the assessor.

faqs.q: When are Tulsa County taxes due?
faqs.a: At least half before January 1 and the second half before April 1. Missing the first-half deadline makes the full amount due and subject to delinquent tax rules.
